 Description 
 
Epic 1 — Platform Foundation. Migration story — the team is already deploying onto the Day-0 CloudFormation cluster while you swap it for a Terraform-managed one.

Working with AI on this project
Read Working with AI first — it covers how to work with Claude Code, the subscription cap, and the standard deliverables (including the required WORKING-WITH-AI.md memoir). This ticket only adds the story-specific pieces.

Story
Problem statement
Framing for the team: the Day-0 cluster was built with CloudFormation because that's how it was originally done at this fictional company. The decision to migrate to Terraform is yours to defend — your PM (and a future interviewer) will ask "why did you have a need to create Terraform code for launching the EKS cluster when CloudFormation already worked?" Have an answer.
The team's EKS cluster currently exists as a CloudFormation-managed stack — {{temporary-eks-cluster-$
{ENVIRONMENT_STAGE}}} — brought up manually by the coordinator. It works; your teammates are already deploying onto it. Your job is to migrate it to Terraform without disrupting them:

# Build a parallel Terraform-managed cluster in the same dev account, and modernize what was defensible-but-not-great in the CFN setup:make it IPv6-primary with nodes in private subnets and IPv6 egress (no NAT, no public IPv4 on nodes). The CFN cluster ran nodes in public subnets with a public IPv4 each — it worked, but AWS now charges for public IPv4 and that line item is visible on the team's bill. The migration is partly "port it to Terraform" and partly_"stop paying for IPv4."_
# Plan and execute a cutover so teammates' workloads keep working (or are scheduled for a brief flag day they're warned about).
# Decommission the CloudFormation stack once the new cluster is verified.
# Fill in the shared deploy-platform-tools.yaml workflow so it logs into your cluster (it ships as comments only — sequenced with other stories touching that file).

This is a migration, not a greenfield build. The interview narrative isn't "I wrote Terraform for an EKS cluster" — it's "I migrated a running cluster between infrastructure tools without taking down the team, and cut the IPv4 bill doing it." The runbook, validation, and rollback plan are the deliverable; the Terraform is a sub-deliverable.

h3. What you're walking into

Read the Day-0 scaffold every team starts from (repos, empty stubs, OIDC-only IAM, the manual cluster, Terraform conventions). Specific to this story:

* The cluster you're migrating off is a CloudFormation stack,{{temporary-eks-cluster-${ENVIRONMENT_STAGE}
}}, that the coordinator brings up manually from the terminal (not via any workflow). Its CFN templates + Makefile live in the platform-tools repo under{{eks-cloudformation/}}; worker nodes are spot-priced in public subnets with a public IPv4 each. Read it before you replicate its shape.
	•	K8s admin auth on it is the aws-auth ConfigMap, granting admin to the SSO Administrator role. Your cluster must reach parity (see acceptance criteria).
	•	deploy-platform-tools.yaml ships as comments only — it does not point at anything yet. Part of your migration is filling it in so it logs into your cluster (aws eks update-kubeconfig --name <your-cluster>).
	•	Other Epic-1 teammates build on top of you: 1.2 (IAM roles + access-entry mappings), 1.3 (ALB Controller + Gateway API), 1.4 (Karpenter on your base ASG), 1.5 (cert-manager / external-dns / Secrets CSI).
	•	App-delivery teammates (3.1 / 3.3 / 3.5) are already deploying onto the CFN cluster in week 1 and won't pause — your cutover handles a moving target.
Your own-branch work
Build a VPC and an EKS cluster as two custom Terraform modules in{{terraform-infra-<BATCH>-<TEAM>}}, called from{{roots/environments/dev/main.tf}} (VPC first — EKS consumes its outputs), deployed via a terraform-deploy.yaml GHA workflow you write yourself (plus a destroy-on-PR-approval workflow). The conventions (root-per-env, no off-the-shelf modules, S3 native locking, branch model) are in the Day-0 scaffold.
You own the module design — resource layout, naming, variables, how the two wire together, and how you debug it. The constraints below don't move, though: most are line items on the team's real AWS bill (public IPv4, NAT, instance size, node count, on-demand ratio), and this project runs on a budget the PM is watching. Treat them as requirements, not starting suggestions — deviating up is overprovisioning, not initiative.
Bootstrap (one-time, local with SSO creds). Nothing IAM-shaped exists to let GHA apply your Terraform, so you break the chicken-and-egg from your laptop:
	1	aws sso login with the coordinator-issued profile.
	2	Create the S3 state-backend bucket by hand (aws s3 mb ... + versioning).
	3	Apply a small bootstrap/ module that creates a minimal GHA Terraform IAM role — OIDC trust scoped to your repo + dev environment, just enough permissions to apply the rest.
	4	Set its ARN as the IAM_ROLE env var on the dev GitHub environment.
From there GHA runs every apply. This role is ad-hoc — Story 1.2 later PRs in the canonical shared role to replace it, so don't over-build it. Document the bootstrap in your runbook.
VPC module.
	•	IPv4 CIDR (unique across the org) plus an IPv6 CIDR (Amazon /56 or BYOIP — IPv6 is required).
	•	3 public + 3 private subnets across 3 AZs.
	•	Private subnets: IPv6-primary, nodes-only, outbound via an*Egress-Only IGW*, no public IPv4. (This is where the per-node IPv4 charge dies.)
	•	Public subnets: dual-stack, LB-only — for future ALBs / NLBs.
	•	No NAT Gateway. Standard IGW for the public subnets; EIGW for IPv6 egress from private subnets.
	•	Must also support RDS later (3.x) — confirm those engine versions do IPv6 or plan to dual-stack the DB subnets; note it in the README.
EKS module.
	•	K8s version one release behind the latest EKS supports (verify on deploy day).
	•	IPv6-primary (kubernetesNetworkConfig.ipFamily = ipv6), VPC CNI configured for IPv6 pods.
	•	Nodes in private subnets, no public IPv4, outbound via EIGW.
	•	Self-managed ASG (no managed node groups), t3.medium-class,mixed 20% on-demand / 80% spot, 0 base on-demand, min 1 / max 5 / desired 3, multi-AZ.
	•	Add-ons via Terraform: VPC CNI (IPv6) + EBS CSI (plus any the version requires).
	•	Security groups: minimal rules, only control-plane ↔ node ↔ API — and allow IPv6 where the CFN cluster had IPv4 rules.
	•	This ASG hosts platform tools only (Karpenter, cert-manager, ingress); Karpenter (1.4) handles workload scaling later. Size for platform tools, not apps.
EKS access entries (not aws-auth). Use access entries — the modern model. Day-one parity = admin for at least the SSO Administrator role and your bootstrap GHA role. Story 1.2 layers Developer/DevOps
	•	the canonical role on later. Coordinate with 1.2 on where access-entry config lives (your EKS module vs. their IAM module) — pick one.
IPv6 decisions doc (1–2 pages, graded). Subnet topology and why; EIGW vs NAT; which AWS services you confirmed do IPv6; known reachability gaps (see gotchas); the IPv4 cost math (before / after / what remains). Present it to teammates (~15 min) — explaining it is the point.
The migration (the actual story). Write a migration runbook before cutover:
	•	Parallel-run window — how long both clusters coexist, who deploys where during it.
	•	Validation — how you show the new cluster is equivalent (diff add-ons, deploy a canary, confirm access-entry parity).
	•	Cutover — fill in deploy-platform-tools.yaml so it logs into your cluster; coordinate with 3.1 / 3.3 / 3.5 to redeploy onto it.
	•	Rollback — how long the CFN cluster stays alive, who calls it.
	•	Decommission — tear the CFN stack down (make destroy) once burned in.
You own the decisions in the runbook (window length, rollback criteria, cutover scheduling); Claude can draft it. deploy-platform-tools.yaml is shared — see gotchas for merge sequencing.
Acceptance criteria
	•	Bootstrap done locally: S3 state bucket + minimal ad-hoc GHA Terraform role created, ARN set as IAM_ROLE on the dev GitHub environment. All subsequent applies run via your{{terraform-deploy.yaml}} workflow, not your laptop.
	•	VPC + EKS are two custom modules (no off-the-shelf) called from roots/environments/dev/main.tf; all three env roots exist with the same module-call shape.
	•	The cost guards hold: no NAT Gateway, no public IPv4 on nodes (IPv6-primary, private nodes via Egress-Only IGW), and a*self-managed mixed spot/on-demand ASG sized for platform tools only* — no managed node groups, nothing bigger or more numerous than the EKS-module spec above.
	•	EKS is IPv6-primary, one version behind latest, with*access entries at CFN* aws-auth parity (SSO Administrator role + your bootstrap GHA role).
	•	Migration runbook: bootstrap, parallel-run window, validation, cutover, rollback, decommission, before/after IPv4 cost snapshot.
	•	IPv6 decisions doc (1–2 pp) + a ~15-min teammate walkthrough.
	•	deploy-platform-tools.yaml filled in to log into your cluster (PR into platform-tools, sequenced with other stories).
	•	All CFN-cluster workloads migrated with owner ack; CFN stack decommissioned by demo day (no orphans).
	•	README screenshots: cluster, version, mixed-instance nodes, access-entries list.
Deliverables
	1	bootstrap/ module + the runbook section on the local-with-SSO first apply.
	2	VPC + EKS modules and roots/environments/dev/ wiring (skeleton{{staging/}} + production/), merged to main.
	3	terraform-deploy.yaml + destroy-on-PR-approval workflows.
	4	README — overview, architecture diagram (IPv6 / private-subnet / EIGW topology), issues faced, run instructions (incl. the bootstrap dance), screenshots.
	5	WORKING-WITH-AI.md memoir.
	6	Migration runbook (see acceptance criteria for contents).
	7	IPv6 decisions doc (1–2 pp).
	8	Cutover PR wiring deploy-platform-tools.yaml to your cluster.
Demo (what you walk the PM through)
	1	Whiteboard: why migrate from CFN to Terraform on this team specifically — and why IPv6 + private subnets — grounded in this project's constraints (the IPv4 line item), not generic IaC talking points.
	2	Live: kubectl get nodes on the Terraform cluster — mixed spot/on-demand, multi-AZ, no public IPv4 (private IPv4 + IPv6 only).
	3	Live: pod IPs are IPv6, and a pod reaches the internet (curl -6 https://api.github.com).
	4	Live: the EKS access entries, and how they map to the same identities the CFN aws-auth ConfigMap did.
	5	Walk the runbook: the parallel-run window and why; the validation checks and outcomes; the rollback plan; the before/after IPv4 cost snapshot.
	6	The deploy-platform-tools.yaml you filled in to log into your cluster, and the PR that merged it, sequenced with other stories.
	7	The CFN stack no longer exists (aws cloudformation list-stacks ... or the console).
	8	Anything from the memoir (§3 what Claude got wrong, §4 what I verified) worth surfacing.
Gotchas & references
Read Story 1.1 — gotchas before you start, and keep it open while you work. It's a long list on purpose — this is a real migration, and the traps, cross-team coordination points, and doc links in there are most of what separates "it deployed" from "I understood what I shipped." The more of them you hit and reason through, the better.

 Description 
 
Epic 1 — Platform Foundation. Cross-work normalization story — touches both other teammates' branches in the infra repo and other teammates' separate app repos.

Working with AI on this project
Read Working with AI before you start. It is the same for every story and covers: how to direct Claude (and why re-typing what it can generate isn't the skill being graded), the subscription-cap discipline, the standard deliverables (code, README, and the required WORKING-WITH-AI.md memoir), and how the work splits between you and the AI. This ticket only adds the story-specific pieces below.

Story
Problem statement
Framing for the team: this story is happening "as per request from the external Security audit team/contractors." You are not just shipping IAM — you are answering an audit, and you will defend your design to a stakeholder (your PM) as if they were the audit team.
You are the team's IAM owner. You have three jobs:
	1	Build out the team-wide identity layer the scaffold doesn't cover: Developer and DevOps roles for dev and prod accounts, plus the Kubernetes-side access entries that let a developer user have read-only access on the cluster while CI/CD systems have what they need.
	2	Own the canonical shared GHA Terraform IAM role. Story 1.1 bootstrapped a minimal ad-hoc version to unblock itself; you design the canonical one (tightly-scoped trust + a permission set sized for all the project's Terraform) and submit a consolidation PR into 1.1's branch that swaps theirs for yours.
	3	Normalize across your teammates' work — both the ad-hoc roles on other infra-repo branches (1.4 Karpenter, 4.1 GitLab runner, …) and the per-app roles app-delivery teammates (3.1 / 3.3 / 3.5) created by hand in the AWS console. Consolidate all of them into one scheme. (Detail in Cross-work normalization below.)
The normalization is the deliverable, not a side-effect. The interview narrative is "I worked across five engineers' work — three app repos and two infra-repo branches — to consolidate ad-hoc IAM roles."
What you're walking into
Read the Day-0 scaffold — the key fact for you: the GitHub OIDC provider is the only IAM thing that pre-exists; you build every role. SSO / IdP is coordinator-managed (you don't touch it). Specific to this story:
	•	From Story 1.1: 1.1's owner bootstrapped a minimal ad-hoc GHA Terraform IAM role (local-with-SSO) whose ARN currently sits in the{{IAM_ROLE}} env var on the dev GitHub environment of{{terraform-infra-<BATCH>-<TEAM>}}. Designing its canonical replacement and PR-ing it into 1.1's branch is your job (below). 1.1's cluster uses EKS access entries (not aws-auth) — coordinate with 1.1 on which roles get K8s access.
	•	From other infra-repo branches (1.x / 4.x): teammates may have minted their own ad-hoc IAM roles (Karpenter in 1.4, the GitLab runner in 4.1, …). They live on their feature branches. Read them.
	•	From app-delivery teammates (3.1 / 3.3 / 3.5): each works in a_separate app repo_ and likely created their per-app role manually in the AWS console in week 1; their workflow YAML / GH environment references it by ARN/name. You won't find these in your infra repo — locate them via aws iam list-roles and each app repo's workflows.
	•	EKS access entries: teammates may add entries manually as they need cluster access. Don't fight it in week 1; normalize during consolidation.
Your own-branch work
Build the team-wide identity layer as Terraform managed by GitHub Actions.
The role spec below is the audit's starting point, not a recipe to type out. You own the design and — more to the point — the why behind every boundary, which you defend to the PM as if to the auditor. Where the spec is explicit it's because the audit requires it; where it's silent, the call is yours.
AWS IAM:
Five role classes required:
	•	DeveloperDevAccessRole — read permissions on all EC2 actions, EKS, and full access to S3.
	•	DevopsDevAccessRole — full permissions.
	•	DeveloperProdAccessRole — read permissions on EC2, EKS, and S3.
	•	DevopsProdAccessRole — full read permissions in Prod (except for secrets) and full permissions on EC2.
	•	SharedGHATerraformRole (or whatever you name it) — the*canonical shared role GHA assumes* to apply Terraform across the project. Trust policy: OIDC from{{token.actions.githubusercontent.com}}, subject scoped to the team's terraform-infra-<BATCH><TEAM> repo and dev GitHub environment (extendable to platform-tools<BATCH>-<TEAM> if another story needs Terraform there). Permission set: scoped to what all Terraform in the project needs — broader than 1.1's bootstrap role, narrower than AdministratorAccess. This role replaces 1.1's ad-hoc bootstrap role via your cross-work PR.
The four human/access roles must trust the parent AWS account:879500880845. The shared GHA role uses the OIDC provider, not the parent account. (Per-app GHA roles — ECR push, Secrets Manager read — come out of the cross-work normalization below.)
Prod environment on this project. Per-team prod accounts don't exist during the final project. Deploy the prod roles into the same dev account but in the roots/environments/production/ root module — with -prod suffixes on names so they don't collide with the dev-root roles. To test creation of prod roles: in your{{feature/}} branch, temporarily flip your workflow's{{ENVIRONMENT_STAGE}} to production so it applies the production root against the dev account. (This works because we have one root per env, each with its own state file — not a shared root with swappable tfvars.)
Trust policy scoping. Tight: SSO-group → role for human users, OIDC → role for GHA workflows. No * wildcards on the principal account or subject patterns.
How an SSO user actually assumes one of your roles (the part that's easy to leave implicit and worth getting right):
IAM Identity Center logs the developer in as an{{AWSReservedSSO_<PermissionSet><hash>}} role under the account's{{aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/<REGION>/}} path. To let _that role assume your DeveloperDevAccessRole, your trust policy needs to reference the SSO role ARN with a wildcard suffix (the _<hash> changes if the permission set is ever recreated):
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Principal": { "AWS": "arn:aws:iam::879500880845:root" },
    "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
    "Condition": {
      "ArnLike": {
        "aws:PrincipalArn":
          "arn:aws:iam::879500880845:role/aws-reserved/sso.amazonaws.com/us-east-1/AWSReservedSSO_DeveloperBase_*"
      }
    }
  }]
}
The matching gate on the SSO side — letting the developer's permission set call sts:AssumeRole against roles in the team's account — is set up by the project coordinator once, scoped to a naming convention (so engineers can self-serve new roles inside the account without going back to the SSO admin every time).
sts:SetSourceIdentity — include in both the permission set's allow list and your role's trust policy Action array. This lets CloudTrail record the human behind a chained assume-role session, which is what an auditor wants.
No off-the-shelf modules. MUST NOT use community Terraform modules from GitHub or the Terraform Registry (e.g.terraform-aws-modules/iam/aws). Write your own — the point is to learn IAM, not to wrap someone else's abstraction.
Defensible boundaries. Beyond the starting-point spec, you own the why: why does a developer get read on S3 but not write? Why does DevOps-Prod exclude secrets? You will defend each boundary in the design doc and the demo.
Kubernetes-side mapping:
	•	The cluster's EKS access entries map the DeveloperProdAccessRole IAM role to a Kubernetes group with view permissions cluster-wide and no write permissions.
	•	Explicitly forbid kubectl exec and access to Kubernetes Secret objects for the developer group. Why both matter:
	◦	If a developer can kubectl exec into a pod, they can printenv and read whatever credentials the application injected as env vars. That defeats the no-secrets restriction.
	◦	Direct access to Secret objects (e.g. kubectl get secret -o yaml) leaks the same credentials a different way.
	•	Use Kubernetes RBAC: ClusterRole + ClusterRoleBinding for precise control. Don't grant via aggregated roles or view defaults without checking — view includes Secret read in some versions.
	•	DevOps IAM role mapped to a group with broader (but still scoped) access.
	•	Coordinate with Story 1.1's owner on where exactly this lives in the Terraform code (does access-entries config live in 1.1's cluster module, or in your IAM module that consumes the cluster?).
	•	Deployment. Your K8s user-role config deploys via the{{deploy-platform-tools.yaml}} workflow in the platform-tools repo — which ships as comments only, so you fill in / append your section. It's a shared file several stories fill in — sequence your merges (see gotchas).
A design doc (1–2 pages) explaining the role boundaries and why. This is the artifact you defend in your demo.
Cross-work normalization
The deliverable that doesn't live on your branch. Same job in two flavors — infra-repo branches vs. separate app repos — run as four phases:
	1	Observe (late wk 1 → early wk 2). Find every ad-hoc IAM role. Inside the infra repo, diff teammates' branches (git diff main...origin/feature/STORY-1.4-karpenter – '.tf') —*start with 1.1's bootstrap role, the guaranteed first target. Across app repos, find the console-created roles (aws iam list-roles) and the workflow/env that references them. For each: permissions, trust policy, overscoped? duplicated?
	2	Design (early wk 2). A unified scheme: the canonical{{SharedGHATerraformRole}} (sized for all project Terraform), a small set of parameterised app roles (one per purpose — ECR push, Secrets Manager read — e.g. App-<app><purpose>-Role<env>), and trust templates (SSO ArnLike for humans, OIDC for GHA). Document it in the design doc.
	3	Ship the cutovers (wk 2 → 3). Infra-repo: a PR into each teammate's feature branch swapping their role for a call to your module. App repos: a small PR pointing the workflow / GH env at the canonical role name (manifests unchanged); once it merges, the owner deletes the manual console role.
	4	Decommission. Confirm every ad-hoc role — branch and console — is gone (aws iam list-roles); record each in the cutover ledger.
Acceptance criteria
	•	Four human/access roles (DeveloperDevAccessRole,DevopsDevAccessRole, DeveloperProdAccessRole,DevopsProdAccessRole) + the canonical SharedGHATerraformRole, all Terraform-managed via GHA, no off-the-shelf IAM modules. Human roles trust 879500880845; the shared role's OIDC trust is scoped tight to the repo + dev.
	•	Canonical app CI/CD roles exist — a small parameterised set (e.g. ECR push, Secrets Manager read), Terraform-managed, one per app-side purpose. These are what the app repos point at — distinct from SharedGHATerraformRole, which is for Terraform applies.
	•	Consolidation PR into 1.1's branch swaps the ad-hoc bootstrap role for the canonical one — merged or in review by demo day, with the dev IAM_ROLE env var repointed.
	•	A cross-work PR into every other source — each infra-repo branch with an ad-hoc role, and each app repo (3.1 / 3.3 / 3.5) pointing its workflow/env at the canonical app role — submitted, merged or in review by demo day.
	•	Prod roles testable end-to-end (deployed via{{roots/environments/production/}}, -prod-suffixed).
	•	SSO trust verified end-to-end: a developer assumes{{DeveloperDevAccessRole}} and can do reads but not write/delete; via that role kubectl get pods works but kubectl delete,exec, and get secret are denied.
	•	Trust policies use the SSO ArnLike pattern (no hard-coded hash) and tightly-scoped OIDC subjects — no * on principal or subject.
	•	Access-model design doc (≤2 pp) explains the boundaries and the shared role's permission set.
	•	No orphaned IAM roles after decommission (aws iam list-roles).
Deliverables
	1	Terraform code for IAM roles + EKS access entries (your own branch in the infra repo, merged to main).
	2	README in your story folder.
	3	WORKING-WITH-AI.md memoir (required — see template).
	4	Access model design doc (1–2 pages).
	5	Cross-work cutovers ledger (a markdown file or a section of the README) with two tables:
	◦	Cross-branch (infra repo): one row per teammate's feature branch you submitted a consolidation PR into, with link + status.
	◦	Cross-repo (app repos + console): one row per app repo you submitted a workflow/env PR into, with link + status + a note that the manually-created console role was deleted.
	6	Reusable IAM module/pattern (committed in a location both your code and other infra-repo teammates' code can import from).
Demo (what you walk the PM through)
	1	Whiteboard the access model — why these roles and boundaries, including the shared role's permission set. PM will probe.
	2	Live: SSO-login as a developer — kubectl get pods works,kubectl delete / exec / get secret fail. Show the trust policy that makes it true.
	3	The consolidation, before/after: 1.1's branch (ad-hoc bootstrap role → canonical SharedGHATerraformRole, IAM_ROLE repointed), and one app repo (manual console-role ARN → canonical role name, then deleted).
	4	Walk the cross-work cutovers ledger (both tables).
	5	Anything from the memoir (§3 what Claude got wrong, §4 what I verified) worth surfacing.
Gotchas & references
Read Story 1.2 — gotchas before you start, and keep it open while you work. It's a long list on purpose — this is an audit response, and the audit-failure patterns, cross-team coordination points, and doc links in there are most of what separates "the roles exist" from "I can defend this design." The more of them you hit and reason through, the better.

Epic 1 — Platform Foundation. Migration + cross-work normalization story — you swap the team's traffic plane off the Day-0 ingress-nginx onto Gateway API, and submit the per-app Ingress → HTTPRoute cutover PRs into your app-delivery teammates' branches. No single predecessor ticket; it shares the platform-tools deploy conventions used across the platform stories.

Working with AI on this project
Read Working with AI first — it covers how to work with Claude Code, the subscription cap, and the standard deliverables (including the required WORKING-WITH-AI.md memoir). This ticket only adds the story-specific pieces.

Story
Problem statement
Framing for the team: the Day-0 traffic plane is ingress-nginx with classic Ingress resources, installed by hand. It works — your teammates are already serving traffic through it. The decision to migrate is yours to defend: your PM (and a future interviewer) will ask "*why move off ingress-nginx when it works?" Have an answer that's about this team, not generic "Gateway API is the future" talk.*
ingress-nginx is in maintenance mode; Gateway API is the modern, role-oriented replacement (the Gateway is owned by you, the platform owner; each HTTPRoute is owned by the app team — which maps exactly to how this team is actually split). Your job is to*migrate the team to Gateway API on the AWS Load Balancer Controller without taking anyone's app down*:
	1	Install the Gateway API CRDs and the AWS Load Balancer Controller (with Gateway API support enabled), and stand up at least one shared team Gateway. ALBs land in the public, dual-stack, LB-only subnets Story 1.1 built for exactly this.
	2	Publish HTTPRoute conventions so teammates know how to attach their app to the shared Gateway.
	3	Submit the per-app cutover PRs (classic Ingress →HTTPRoute) into each K8s app-delivery teammate's feature branch and main, preserving their existing path matchers and backends.
	4	Decommission ingress-nginx once every app has migrated.
This is a migration, not a greenfield install. The interview narrative isn't "I installed an ingress controller" — it's "I migrated my team's whole traffic plane off legacy ingress-nginx onto Gateway API + ALB, including the per-app cutover PRs into three engineers' branches." The migration plan, the conventions doc, and the cutover ledger are the deliverable; the manifests are a sub-deliverable.
What you're walking into
Read the Day-0 scaffold every team starts from (repos, empty stubs, OIDC-only IAM, the manual cluster, Terraform conventions, PR rules). Specific to this story:

Yours has to be specific: what to flag vs. what to ignore, and how strictly to score the requirements checklist against the ticket's acceptance criteria (over-strict fails everything; over-lenient rubber-stamps). You tune it against real PRs until the output is useful, not noisy — and you keep a prompt-tuning log of what you tried, what worked, and what didn't. The honest narrative is that you spent more time on the prompt than on the wiring.
The three bespoke outputs, posted as a PR comment:
	•	Line-level review comments on the diff.
	•	A requirements-met checklist scored against the resolved ticket's acceptance criteria — the part that makes this more than a linter.
	•	Demo Q&A — the "stakeholder questions you should be ready for" drafts, written for a different reader (the PM / a teammate prepping their demo), not the PR author.
Acceptance criteria
	•	Installed across every repo the team works in (infra + each app repo), triggered on PR open and gated so it doesn't re-fire on every commit; the Anthropic API key is a secret, never committed.
	•	Implementation choice is defended — you can say what you used, what you considered, and why (the ticket doesn't pin a tool).
	•	Resolves the Jira ticket from the PR description — extracts the key, fetches the ticket — and scores the diff against that ticket's acceptance criteria; degrades gracefully when no ticket resolves.
	•	Posts all three outputs as a PR comment: line-level comments, a requirements-met checklist, and demo Q&A.
	•	Runs on at least 5 real PRs across the team's repos, correctly resolving each PR's ticket and scoring against its criteria.
	•	PM agrees the output was useful in at least 3 of those.
	•	The demo-Q&A draft is in use by at least one teammate prepping their demo.
	•	Prompt-tuning log — what you tried, what worked, what didn't, and how the output got less noisy.
	•	README with issues faced, the implementation you chose (and why), and how the reviewer + prompt are wired across the repos.
Deliverables
	1	The reviewer config — the workflow(s) installed in each repo, the ticket-resolution piece, and your review prompt files.
	2	Prompt-tuning log — the iteration record (the graded judgment artifact, like 5.1's autonomy memo / 5.3's security model).
	3	README — overview, the implementation you chose and why, how it's wired across the team's repos, issues faced.
	4	WORKING-WITH-AI.md memoir.
Demo (what you walk the PM through)

	2	Live: open a PR (or re-run on a real one); watch the reviewer resolve the Jira ticket from the description and post the three outputs — and show it's live in more than one of the team's repos, not just one.
	3	Show the requirements-met checklist scored against the ticket's acceptance criteria — and a case where it correctly flags a missing requirement.
	4	Show the demo Q&A a teammate actually used to prep, and the graceful-degrade path when a PR has no resolvable ticket.
	5	Show the API key is a secret, not in git.
	6	Anything from the memoir (§3 what Claude got wrong, §4 what I verified) worth surfacing.

It's a long list on purpose — the prompt-tuning (useful vs. noisy), the brittle ticket resolution, the honest-scoring problem, and the shared-API-key cost discipline are most of what separates "the reviewer ran" from "the team actually reads its output," and they're the best interview material in this ticket.  Description 
 
Epic 5 — AI Ops. A build-and-own story: give the team's Claude Code a least-privilege way to read the platform and act on it through MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers — and own the security model for what an AI agent is allowed to touch. The servers are mostly off-the-shelf; the design of who can connect and what each one can do is the graded heart.

Working with AI on this project
Read Working with AI first — it covers how to work with Claude Code, the subscription cap, and the standard deliverables (including the required WORKING-WITH-AI.md memoir). This ticket only adds the story-specific pieces.

Story
Problem statement
Framing for the team: your teammates already use Claude Code on this project. Your job is to make it talk to the team's own platform directly — read Grafana/Prometheus/the cluster, log progress to Jira, spin up a test pod on request — instead of everyone copy-pasting{{kubectl}} output into a chat. Your PM (and a future interviewer) will ask the hard version: "*you've handed an AI agent a button that can change the live cluster — what stops it, or a leaked token, from doing damage?" The security model is your answer, and it's what's graded.*
Stand up the team's MCP layer: one read-only data MCP and one mutating MCP, callable from any team member's Claude Code, demonstrated against real tasks. This is not a "write two servers" story — where an official server already exists, you install, deploy, secure, and operate it; you build your own only where no official server covers the need. The two auth boundaries you design — who may connect to each server, and what each server is itself allowed to do — are the graded deliverable; the servers are the realistic thing you prove them on.
What you're walking into
Read the Day-0 scaffold every team starts from (repos, empty stubs, OIDC-only IAM, the manual cluster, Terraform conventions, PR rules). Specific to this story:
	•	The cluster-hosted server runs on the team's EKS cluster (Story 1.1). You consume it; you don't build it. The cluster is*IPv6-primary with IPv6-only egress* from the nodes — read 1.1's IPv6 decisions doc, because it shapes anything your server calls out to at runtime (see gotchas).
	•	Your read-only MCP is local and unblocked. The read-only data MCP runs as a local stdio server in each member's Claude Code config — no cluster hosting, real week-1 work that waits on nothing. The*mutating MCP* is the in-cluster, security-heavy piece (deployment + public URL + the two auth boundaries).
	•	MCP is recent and not pre-taught. Like ArgoCD on 4.2, the tooling at the centre of your story isn't in the curriculum — budget for learning it, and turn what you learn into the security model doc.
	•	This is a build-and-own story, not a cross-work normalization one. No four-phase observe/design/ship/decommission, no PRs into teammates' branches. Your cluster-hosted server's public exposure tracks the team traffic plane (1.3/1.5) and you adopt it yourself — it is not sent to you as a cutover PR (those target the 3.x app-delivery branches, and you're not one). See the gotchas for the contract.
Your work
The decisions below are yours to make and defend; the constraints that don't move are called out.
What you deliver: exactly two MCPs — one read-only data MCP and*one mutating MCP*. For each, use the official server if one exists (Grafana, Prometheus, Atlassian/Jira, and Kubernetes all ship MCP servers today); only build your own where no official server covers the need. Reinventing a shipped server burns the time the security model and the MCP-vs-CLI case deserve.
Read-only data MCP — local stdio. Pick one: a Grafana, Prometheus, or kubectl-read MCP. Runs in each member's Claude Code config. Choose with the dependency in mind: a Grafana/Prometheus MCP needs 2.1's stack to exist first; a kubectl-read MCP works against the cluster from day one.
Mutating MCP — cluster-hosted, in-cluster. This is the security-heavy one, and it's deliberately the cluster kind — e.g. a "spin me a test pod" server — because that's where the hosting and the two auth boundaries live. Build one (to own its scope) or deploy an official Kubernetes MCP and scope it — either way you own its blast radius. It's a Deployment + Service in the cluster; if you build a server, its image goes to ECR from GitHub Actions (git-SHA tags). (A_SaaS_ mutating MCP — say a Jira progress logger over the official Atlassian MCP — would run local and skip all the hosting and auth work, which is exactly why your required mutating MCP is the cluster one. Wire a SaaS one too if you want, but it doesn't substitute.)
MCP vs CLI — research it and make the case. An MCP is not automatically better than the tool it wraps. For each MCP you deliver, work out when it actually beats just running the CLI — and where it doesn't (added latency, one more moving part to secure, drift from the underlying tool). This goes in your docs and you argue it in the demo; "I wrapped kubectl because I could" is not the answer.
Two auth boundaries — the graded heart. Design and document both:
	•	Client → MCP (how teammates reach the cluster-hosted server): a*bearer token checked at the edge is the required baseline* — each teammate adds the remote server to Claude Code with a bearer header; the server URL can live in the team's project-scoped .mcp.json, but the token comes from an env var and is never committed. An OAuth flow (oauth2-proxy in front of an IdP) is more secure but more complex — flag it as the stronger alternative; it is not required.
	•	MCP → platform (what the server may do): a tightly-scoped Kubernetes ServiceAccount + RBAC Role (e.g. create pods in one namespace, nothing cluster-wide), plus IRSA / Pod Identity with a tight policy for any AWS call — never *. Credentials live server-side, never on a laptop.
Traffic plane for the cluster-hosted server is yours to own. You write the HTTPRoute and wire the TLS cert yourself, coordinating with the 1.3 and 1.5 owners — see the gotchas for the contract. Reachable at{{mcp-<TEAM>-dev.<TEAM_DOMAIN>}}.
Cost — bound what the agent can create (non-negotiable). The mutating MCP's whole job is creating cluster resources on request — so a careless prompt or a leaked token could create big or many of them and run up the team's real dev bill. Cap it: resource limits and a namespace quota on what it's allowed to create, so the blast radius has a cost ceiling, not just a permissions one. (The server itself is a single small pod on the existing nodes — that part's negligible; the spend risk is in what it creates.)
Acceptance criteria
	•	Two MCPs callable from any team member's Claude Code: a read-only data MCP and a (cluster-hosted) mutating MCP.
	•	Read-only data MCP runs as a local stdio server and is demoed against real tasks.
	•	Mutating MCP deployed in-cluster, on the existing nodes, reachable at mcp-<TEAM>-dev.<TEAM_DOMAIN> over the internet,behind a bearer-token check — no unauthenticated mutating endpoint exposed.
	•	Least privilege proven: the mutating server runs under a scoped ServiceAccount that can do only what it's meant to (show an out-of-scope action being denied by RBAC), with IRSA/Pod Identity for any AWS call, and a resource-limit / quota ceiling so it can't run up the bill with what it creates.
	•	MCP-vs-CLI case made in the docs and in the demo: for each MCP, where it beats the CLI and where it doesn't.
	•	No tokens or credentials in plaintext in any repo — server URL in .mcp.json, token from an env var.
	•	Exposure tracks the traffic plane, written by you: HTTP via scaffold ingress in week 1; HTTPRoute on the team Gateway once 1.3 lands; TLS + external-dns once 1.5 lands — authored by you in coordination with 1.3/1.5, not received as a cutover PR.
	•	Security model doc: the two auth boundaries, a per-MCP blast-radius analysis ("what could this do if the token leaked"), and the token issuance / rotation / revocation story.
	•	At least 3 real-task demonstrations recorded that show the MCPs saving time vs. running the tool by hand.
	•	README with issues faced and per-MCP install instructions.
Deliverables

	3	Security model doc — the two auth boundaries + per-MCP blast-radius analysis (including the create-cost ceiling) + token rotation/revocation.
	4	README — overview, the MCP-vs-CLI case for each MCP, issues faced, run/install instructions.
	5	WORKING-WITH-AI.md memoir.
	6	Demo recording — 3 real tasks.
Demo (what you walk the PM through)

Gotchas & references
Read Story 5.3 — gotchas before you start, and keep it open while you work. It's a long list on purpose — the auth boundaries, the "the edge doesn't validate your bearer token for you" trap, and the least-privilege RBAC scoping are most of what separates "the demo worked" from "I designed something I'd let near a real cluster," and they're the best interview material in this ticket.
